focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	Our software company has been at roughly the same revenue for two years.
e002	Not collapsing, not growing—just explaining the same plateau in increasingly sophisticated ways.
e003	The board introduced me to a commercial executive from the largest company in our category.
e004	She has launched products in twenty countries and is interested in becoming our president.
e005	The reaction has been immediate.
e006	Investors are excited, and I can feel the relief in the room whenever her name comes up.
e007	I am the founder and still the CEO.
e008	Maybe this is the leadership we have been missing.
e009	Maybe we are asking a résumé to restore confidence because our own plan did not.
e010	I am having trouble separating those.
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e011	Start with the job, not her name.
e012	What decisions need an owner, what authority would a president actually receive, and which parts of her record could transfer from a much larger company?
e013	The board's relief is information about your company, not yet evidence about her fit.
[Turn 2 USER]
e014	But we do need change.
e015	Sales and product blame each other, nobody owns pricing, and I still jump into large deals.
e016	She saw that quickly and proposed one commercial leader.
e017	I do not want “beware prestige” to become another excuse for us to stay exactly as we are.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e018	Decisiveness has value when ownership is genuinely missing.
e019	Test whether her diagnosis survives contact with your customer economics and product constraints.
e020	Ask for a reconstruction of two hard decisions she made, including what she initially believed, what evidence changed her view, and who bore the cost.
e021	At the same time, decide which interventions you must stop making if you give her the role; otherwise the structure will fail regardless of her ability.
[Turn 3 USER]
e022	She presented a hundred-day plan: interview the top customers, simplify pricing, replace territory-based quotas, and review the product roadmap.
e023	She also wants the authority to change the leadership team after sixty days.
e024	Our head of product says that is too fast and worries that commercial pressure will turn every roadmap argument into a revenue argument.
e025	I told him the existing structure has not earned a veto over change, which he heard as me already taking her side.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e026	The current team's weak performance does not make every proposed pace appropriate.
e027	Separate the authority to recommend changes from a fixed sixty-day judgment about people she has not worked with.
e028	Have her explain how product evidence can override a near-term commercial request and how disagreements with you are resolved.
e029	Your head of product should be heard as a source of operating information, not as a referendum on whether change is needed.
[Turn 4 USER]
e030	I spoke with two references she chose.
e031	Both called her exceptional and said weak performers left after she arrived.
e032	One also said the organization became exhausting for a year, then much stronger.
e033	She described that as the price of raising standards.
e034	I have not spoken with anyone who reported to her and left.
e035	The board chair says senior hires always have detractors and that searching for them can become an excuse not to act.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e036	Those references are useful, but they are also selected witnesses describing the same turnover from the winner's side.
e037	That does not mean the departures were wrong.
e038	It means “weak performers left” is a conclusion you have not independently examined.
e039	Speak with someone who reported to her and left, someone who stayed without being promoted, and someone who depended on her team from outside it.
e040	Ask for concrete decisions, what changed, who absorbed the transition, and what she would now do differently.
e041	Do not run a search for a damaging quote; that would be the mirror image of relying on praise.
e042	You are trying to understand how her method feels and functions when targets are missed, priorities change, and people disagree with her—not to construct a clean reputation.
[Turn 5 USER]
e043	She is willing to spend two paid days with our team on a pricing workshop and let us speak to former direct reports.
e044	She does not want an interim role because she would be leaving a secure job and needs a real mandate.
e045	She has asked for a large equity grant that vests partly when revenue milestones are reached.
e046	Our investors like that alignment.
e047	I worry it could reward contracts that make the product harder to support, but she says we can add a margin condition.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e048	The workshop can reveal how she listens, frames disagreement, and uses evidence, though everyone will behave differently during an audition.
e049	Design the equity around durable company outcomes rather than revenue alone: margin, retention, concentration, or service burden may matter.
e050	More importantly, state which outcomes she controls and which depend on product investment or market conditions, so incentives do not become a substitute for governance.
[Turn 6 USER]
e051	You keep designing safeguards.
e052	That may be my fault for asking this way, but the company needs someone able to break habits.
e053	I am willing to give real authority.
e054	I just cannot yet say where hers ends when we disagree.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e055	Fair correction.
e056	Boundaries are not meant to put a committee around her.
e057	They are how you make delegation real instead of allowing your founder authority to reappear whenever a decision becomes uncomfortable.
e058	Name what she owns, the few reserved decisions, and what happens in a genuine boundary dispute.
[Turn 7 USER]
e059	I am leaning toward continuing to final references and the workshop, then making an offer if we can agree that she owns the commercial organization, pricing execution, and leadership changes within an approved budget.
e060	I would reserve changes to company strategy, major product commitments, and dismissing a founder.
e061	We still need to write how a disputed customer promise is classified, and I want to hear from people who did not succeed under her.
e062	I am more concerned about pretending to delegate than about whether she can produce a confident plan.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e063	That is a more decision-relevant process than choosing between admiration and suspicion.
e064	The next evidence should test how her operating style transfers, while the mandate discussion tests whether the company is prepared to use her ability.
e065	Do not ask adverse references to deliver a verdict; compare concrete patterns across accounts.
e066	Before an offer, resolve the recurring boundary cases and state what each of you can decide without obtaining the other's consent.
[Turn 8 USER]
e067	I found a former regional director who left after eighteen months.
e068	I expected either a warning or reassurance and got neither.
e069	He said she made the organization much more disciplined and that some of the changes were overdue.
e070	He also said she would change priorities without naming what teams had already sacrificed for the previous one.
e071	Eventually people learned to wait for the next message instead of challenging the current plan.
e072	He did not call her dishonest, abusive, or even a bad executive.
e073	She told me the region was missing targets and needed urgency, which is also plausible.
e074	I keep wanting the reference to tell me whether to hire her.
e075	Instead it gave me a behavior I need to understand: when does changing direction create adaptation, and when does it teach people that today's commitment is theater?
[Turn 8 ASSISTANT]
e076	Use the disagreement to form a work test rather than choosing which narrator to trust.
e077	Ask her for a priority she reversed, how she communicated the cost, and what signals told her people were complying without committing.
e078	Ask the former director what challenge channels existed and whether the outcome improved.
e079	The relevant pattern is not whether priorities ever changed, but whether new evidence, accountability, and dissent traveled in both directions.
[Turn 9 USER]
e080	The pricing workshop went well at first.
e081	She asked good questions and found that discounts were compensating for a confusing packaging decision.
e082	Near the end, she asked our head of product whether he was willing to execute a commercial strategy he disagreed with.
e083	He became defensive and said product is not a service department.
e084	I admired that she surfaced the conflict, but I also noticed the room began performing for me once it became clear I was impressed by her.
[Turn 9 ASSISTANT]
e085	The workshop revealed the real boundary and also became a staged social setting.
e086	Debrief participants separately before sharing your view, asking what she understood, oversimplified, and changed in their thinking.
e087	Ask her what she learned from the head of product, not only whether he can execute.
e088	Your visible enthusiasm is now part of the evidence environment, so a unanimous positive debrief would not be self-validating.
[Turn 10 USER]
e089	She has another opportunity and wants a decision within ten days.
e090	The board chair says we have gathered more evidence than most companies do and warns that endless process sends strong candidates away.
e091	My cofounder, who is no longer operating day to day, thinks hiring her would reassure employees that the board still believes we can grow.
e092	That last argument worries me because employee reassurance is not the president's job, yet I understand why the signal matters after two flat years.
[Turn 10 ASSISTANT]
e093	Ten days is enough only if the remaining questions are specific.
e094	Use it for the mandate charter, separate workshop debriefs, and the disagreement process.
e095	Do not let her other offer decide what job exists at your company.
[Turn 11 USER]
e096	The debriefs were mixed but concrete.
e097	Sales felt understood; product thought she jumped too quickly from one pricing example to a reorganization.
e098	She accepted that feedback and rewrote the first thirty days around diagnosis rather than leadership changes.
e099	We also changed the equity proposal: revenue, gross retention, and contribution margin all matter, with no vesting based on a single large contract.
e100	She is asking for the board to approve the authority charter as part of the offer, which I take as a good sign.
[Turn 11 ASSISTANT]
e101	Her response provides better evidence than the original polished plan because it shows how she handles grounded resistance.
e102	The revised incentives reduce one obvious distortion, and board approval makes delegation an organizational commitment rather than a private promise from you.
e103	Still define how the charter changes, who evaluates the mixed outcomes, and what support or exit looks like if the role is structurally sound but the working relationship is not.
[Turn 12 USER]
e104	I will recommend an offer with the board-approved authority charter, the revised outcome mix, and a six-month review of both company results and how decisions travel across the leadership team.
e105	She can change leaders after an initial diagnostic period, but disputed product commitments follow the written boundary process.
e106	I am not treating the workshop or references as proof that she will succeed.
e107	They were enough to replace a prestige-driven yes with a specific bet we can explain, and enough to reveal that my own willingness to delegate is part of that bet.
[Turn 12 ASSISTANT]
e108	The final recommendation names a bet rather than pretending the process delivered certainty.
e109	You are hiring for integrated commercial ownership; giving that role authority; limiting incentives that could reward fragile revenue; and acknowledging that your own behavior can make the structure fail.
e110	Keep the disagreement between references, the individual workshop debriefs, the first plan and its revision, the charter, and the incentive rationale—not just the final board paper.
e111	At six months, ask both what results changed and whether information still travels upward when it is unwelcome.
e112	If the hire works, those records prevent a simple hero story.
e113	If it fails, they help distinguish ability, mandate, founder interference, team resistance, and conditions that changed after the decision.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
